questions.q: What does a backtracking algorithm do when a partial answer breaks a rule?
questions.explain: Backtracking builds a candidate step by step and returns to the previous decision point as soon as the current path cannot work. Filtering at the end is brute force; backtracking avoids exploring dead branches at all.
options: It throws an error and stops
It fixes the partial answer by changing earlier choices at random
It abandons that branch: undoes the last choice and tries the next alternative
It keeps going and filters invalid answers at the end

questions.q: In the choose, explore, undo template, why is the undo step needed?
questions.explain: Changing one shared state going down and changing it back coming up means the whole search needs memory only for the current path. Forget the undo and later branches start from a corrupted state.
options: To free memory for the garbage collector
The same state object is shared by all branches; undo restores it exactly, so the next alternative starts from the correct state
To print the result in reverse order
It is optional and only makes the code clearer

questions.q: Backtracking explores the decision tree in which order, and what does that mean for memory?
questions.explain: Backtracking is a depth-first walk. A tree with a million leaves and depth 20 needs only about 20 levels of state at any moment.
options: Breadth-first; it stores a whole level of partial answers
Depth-first; it only needs the current path, so memory grows with the depth of the tree, not its size
In random order; memory is unpredictable
Level by level from the leaves; it stores every leaf

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The include branch runs before the skip branch at every level. So the first leaf includes everything, then tea without sugar, then sugar without tea, and finally nothing.
options: tea+sugar | tea | sugar | none
none | sugar | tea | tea+sugar
tea | sugar | tea+sugar | none
tea+sugar | sugar | tea | none

questions.q: A shop has 10 coupons and no rules. How many subsets of coupons are there, including "no coupon"?
questions.explain: Each coupon is either in or out: 2 × 2 × … × 2 = 210 = 1,024. 3,628,800 is 10!, the number of orders, which is a different question.

questions.q: How many calls does this include/skip search make for 3 items?
questions.explain: The decision tree has 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15 nodes: 8 leaves (the subsets) and 7 internal decisions. In general 2n + 1 − 1.

questions.q: Why does the subsets function record results.push([...chosen]) instead of results.push(chosen)?
questions.explain: Every stored entry would be the same array object. At the end of the search it is empty, so all results look like []. Store a copy (or a new value such as a joined string).
options: Spread makes the code faster
chosen keeps changing during the search; pushing it stores a reference to the same array, which the undo steps will have emptied by the end
Arrays cannot be stored inside arrays without spread
To sort the results

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both results are the route array itself, which is empty after the last pop. results.push([...route]) would store the two orders.
options: 2 [["Yaba","Ikeja"],["Ikeja","Yaba"]]
2 [["Ikeja","Yaba"],["Ikeja","Yaba"]]

questions.q: This permutation search forgets one undo. What does it print?
questions.explain: used.delete(s) is missing, so every stop stays "used" after its branch. After the first complete route, no branch can choose anything, and the search quietly returns one route instead of six.
options: ABC
ABC ACB BAC BCA CAB CBA
ABC ACB
A B C

questions.q: A rule is monotone for a search that adds items one at a time. What does that mean, and why does it matter?
questions.explain: "At most three coupons" and "discount at most 40%" only get worse as coupons are added. For such rules, pruning at the first violation is safe and cuts off whole subtrees.
options: The rule is checked in sorted order
Once a partial answer breaks the rule, adding more items can never make it valid again, so the branch can be pruned immediately
The rule applies to only one item
The rule is fast to check

questions.q: Marketing adds the rule "a combination must include at least two coupons". What should the search do with it?
questions.explain: This rule is not monotone: adding a coupon fixes it. Pruning on it would cut off every branch at the first step, silently returning nothing. A test comparing the pruned search with brute force catches this immediately.
options: Prune any partial combination with fewer than two coupons
Check it only on complete candidates at the leaves; a partial combination with one coupon can still become valid, so pruning on it would lose valid answers
Ignore it; backtracking cannot handle minimum rules
Reverse the order of the coupons

questions.q: This search wrongly prunes on the rule "at least two items". What does it print?
questions.explain: Without pruning there are 16 subsets, of which 11 have at least two items (16 minus the empty set minus four singles). With the bad prune, every branch has fewer than two items after its first decision and is cut, so nothing is ever found.

questions.q: When generating combinations (bundles where order does not matter), what does passing a start index achieve?
questions.explain: Without it, {rice, oil} and {oil, rice} would both be generated. Choosing only forward from the last index makes the order of choices canonical.
options: It makes the search breadth-first
Each call only chooses items after the last one chosen, so every set is produced once, in one order, instead of once per ordering
It limits the bundle size to start
It sorts the results by price

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each pair appears once, in index order, because the next pick starts after the previous one. C(4, 2) = 4! / (2! × 2!) = 6. The 12-item option is the permutations of two, where order matters.
options: AB AC AD BC BD CD 6
AB AC AD BA BC BD CA CB CD DA DB DC 12
AB BC CD 3
AA AB AC AD BB BC BD CC CD DD 10

questions.q: How many different 2-product bundles can be made from 6 products (order does not matter)?
questions.explain: C(6, 2) = 6 × 5 / 2 = 15. 30 counts ordered pairs (each bundle twice), and 36 also allows the same product twice.

questions.q: The bundle search sorts products by price and, inside its loop, does if (items[i].naira > left) break;. Why break and not continue?
questions.explain: Sorting turns one failed check into a proof about all remaining items, so the loop can stop. continue would still be correct, just slower.
options: Because continue is not allowed in recursive functions
Prices are sorted, so every later product costs at least as much; if this one is too expensive, all the rest are too
To stop the whole search after the first bundle
There is no difference

questions.q: Which bundles cost exactly ₦5,000? What does this print?
questions.explain: The next call starts at i + 1, so each product is used at most once and 2500 + 2500 is impossible. There is no ₦3,000 product to pair with ₦2,000. Bundles are found in index order, so the one starting with ₦1,000 comes first.

questions.q: Why does the permutation search use a used set instead of a start index?
questions.explain: A start index only moves forward, which is right for combinations (order irrelevant) but would only ever produce one ordering. Permutations need "every item not yet used".
options: Sets are faster than numbers
In a permutation order matters, so any unused item may come next, including ones with a smaller index than the last choice
To remove duplicates from the input
A start index would give the same result

questions.q: A rider has 12 stops. How many different visiting orders are there, and what does that say about trying them all?
questions.explain: n! grows faster than 2n: 12! is about 479 million, 15! about 1.3 trillion. Exhaustive route search only works for a handful of stops, even with pruning.
options: 144; trying all is instant
4,096; trying all is fine
479,001,600 (12!); already heavy, and every extra stop multiplies it again
24; only the neighbours matter
1,000,000; a round number

questions.q: What is branch and bound?
questions.explain: It prunes on "cannot be better" rather than "cannot be valid". The route search pruned a partial route when its length plus the distance back to the depot was already at least the best route found.
options: Splitting the input into branches and processing them in parallel
Keeping the best complete answer found so far and abandoning any partial answer whose cost, plus a lower bound on what remains, cannot beat it
Limiting the recursion depth to a fixed bound
Sorting the branches by size

questions.q: In branch and bound, the estimate of the remaining cost must never be more than the true remaining cost. Why?
questions.explain: A valid lower bound guarantees that pruned branches truly cannot win. "You must at least drive back to the depot" never overestimates, so pruning with it keeps the answer exact.
options: So the search finishes faster
If it overestimated, a partial route that could actually win might be pruned, and the search could return a worse answer as "the best"
Because JavaScript numbers overflow
It does not matter; any estimate works

questions.q: The route search can start with best.length set to the greedy route's length plus one. What does that achieve?
questions.explain: Without a starting bound, nothing can be pruned until the first complete route is found. A fast heuristic answer supplies a bound immediately. Using exactly the greedy length would prune an equally short route and could leave best.route empty.
options: It makes the answer greedy instead of optimal
Pruning works from the very first branch, because there is already a good bound; the +1 lets the search still find and record a route of exactly the greedy length
It avoids recursion
It changes which route is shortest

questions.q: Three stops on a line at kilometres 2, 5 and 9, starting from the depot at 0 and returning to it. What does this print?
questions.explain: Driving out to 9 and back is 18 km, and every order that ends at C and returns visits all stops on the way. The first complete route, A, B, C, already achieves 18, and the bound then cuts later branches early: 10 nodes instead of the 16 in the full tree (1 + 3 + 6 + 6). Routes of equal length found later are not recorded, because the check is >=.
options: 18 depot>A>B>C 10
18 depot>A>B>C 16
18 depot>C>B>A 10
16 depot>A>B>C 10

questions.q: In the N-queens solver, why is row - col stored in one set and row + col in another?
questions.explain: Moving down-right adds 1 to both row and column (difference unchanged); moving up-right subtracts 1 from the row and adds 1 to the column (sum unchanged). Sets of those values make the attack check constant time.
options: To store the queen's position twice for safety
All squares on one down-diagonal share the same row - col, and all squares on one up-diagonal share the same row + col, so each diagonal is checked with one O(1) lookup
To count the solutions
Because chessboards are symmetric

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The string lists the column of the queen in each row. On a 4 × 4 board there are exactly two solutions, mirror images of each other. 0123 puts all queens on one diagonal.

questions.q: The sudoku solver chooses the empty cell with the fewest legal digits next. Why does that help so much?
questions.explain: On the classic puzzle the rule needed 51 guesses (one per empty cell, never wrong) against more than 4,000 for the first empty cell. Hard puzzles still need backtracking, but much less.
options: Cells with fewer options are nearer the top of the grid
A cell with one option costs no guessing, and a cell with zero options reveals a dead branch immediately; branching where there are fewest choices keeps the tree small
It guarantees no backtracking ever happens
It makes each check faster

questions.q: When seating guests in a row, the solver only checks the newly seated guest against their left neighbour. Why is that enough?
questions.explain: Checking only what changed keeps the work per node small. Re-validating the whole partial answer at every node gives the same results, just slower.
options: Because only the last pair matters in a seating
Every earlier neighbour pair was already checked when it was formed and has not changed, so only the new pair needs checking, in O(1)
Because forbidden pairs are rare
It is not enough; the whole row must be re-checked each time

questions.q: The product list contains two jars of honey at the same price. The bundle search returns "honey + tea" twice. What is the usual fix?
questions.explain: Skipping equal siblings avoids generating the duplicate branches at all. Deduplicating afterwards also works, but the search still does all the duplicate work, which can be exponential. (If the two jars really are different products for the business, the two bundles are genuinely different.)
options: Remove duplicates from the results with a Set afterwards
Sort the items and, at each depth, skip an item equal to the previous one at the same level: if (i > start && same(items[i], items[i - 1])) continue;
Use permutations instead of combinations
Shuffle the input first
Nothing; the two bundles are different

questions.q: This permutation search stops as soon as it has two results. What does it print?
questions.explain: The search runs only as far as needed: root, A, AB, ABC, ABCD (first result), then ABD, ABDC (second result): 7 calls. The second result returns true, and every level passes it straight up after its undo, so the remaining 58 calls of the full 65-node tree never happen.
options: ABCD ABDC 7
ABCD ABDC 65
ABCD BACD 7
ABCD ABDC 24

questions.q: Which test best catches a pruning rule that silently drops valid answers?
questions.explain: Every answer a bad prune returns may still be valid, so validity checks pass. Only a comparison with the complete list shows what is missing.
options: Checking that every returned answer obeys the rules
Measuring how long the search takes
Comparing the pruned search's results with brute force (generate everything, then filter) on small inputs
Checking that the result list is not empty

questions.q: A checkout runs a backtracking search over coupons on every page load. Marketing plans to add many more coupons. What should the engineers do?
questions.explain: Backtracking is exponential in the worst case. A search that is instant with 7 coupons can hang with 40. Budgets and caps turn a potential outage into a slightly less optimal discount.
options: Nothing; backtracking always finishes quickly
Cap the input size and the number of nodes explored, keep the rule that bounds the depth (at most three coupons), and fall back to the best answer found so far if the budget runs out
Switch to breadth-first search
Cache the results forever

questions.q: A backtracking search for the best van load keeps solving "best load from the remaining items with 40 kg left" in many different branches. What does that suggest?
questions.explain: When different paths lead to the same remaining sub-question, solving it again each time is wasted work. Storing answers by (items left, capacity left) is exactly the knapsack dynamic programming table.
options: The pruning is wrong
The search should be breadth-first
The subproblems overlap; remembering each answer once (dynamic programming) can turn the exponential search into a polynomial one
The input should be shuffled

questions.q: Write allSubsets(items) with backtracking (include, then skip). Return each subset as a string joined with +, and "none" for the empty one. It should print rice+oil+salt rice+oil rice+salt rice oil+salt oil salt none.
questions.explain: Joining at the leaf creates a new string, so no copy of chosen is needed. The include branch comes first, which fixes the output order.
questions.expected: rice+oil+salt rice+oil rice+salt rice oil+salt oil salt none

questions.q: Write bundlesOf(items, k) that returns every k-item bundle (order does not matter) as strings joined with +. It should print tea+milk+sugar tea+milk+bread tea+sugar+bread milk+sugar+bread and then 4.
questions.explain: The start index makes each bundle appear once. C(4, 3) = 4. You could also stop the loop early when too few items remain: i <= items.length - (k - picked.length).

questions.q: Write visitOrders(stops) returning every order of the stops as strings joined with >. It should print 6 and then Yaba>Ikeja>Lekki Yaba>Lekki>Ikeja (the first two).
questions.explain: Two pieces of state (route and used) are changed on the way down, and both must be restored on the way up. 3! = 6 orders.

questions.q: Count the ways to spend exactly ₦6,000 on distinct products (each at most once), with backtracking over prices sorted ascending and a break when a price exceeds what is left. It should print 3.
questions.explain: 1000 + 2000 + 3000, 1000 + 5000 and 2000 + 4000. Only a running total is needed as state, and numbers need no undo because each call gets its own copy of left.

questions.q: Count the solutions of the N-queens puzzle with one queen per row and sets for columns and both diagonals. It should print 1 0 0 2 10 4 for n = 1 to 6.
questions.explain: Boards of size 2 and 3 have no solution: the search explores every option and correctly returns 0. Three sets means three matching deletes in the undo step.

questions.q: Count the valid coupon combinations (including "no coupon") under two monotone rules: at most two coupons, and total discount at most ₦3,000. Prune as soon as a partial combination breaks a rule. It should print 9.
questions.explain: Valid: no coupon (1), each single coupon (4), and the pairs that stay within ₦3,000: 1000 + 500, 1000 + 2000, 2500 + 500 and 500 + 2000 (4). 1000 + 2500 and 2500 + 2000 exceed the limit, and no three coupons are allowed. Both rules only get worse as coupons are added, so pruning on them is safe.

questions.q: The till has limited notes. Find the fewest notes that make an amount exactly, or null, by backtracking over how many of each note to use (most first), pruning branches that already use as many notes as the best found. It should print 3 3 null for ₦600, ₦900 and ₦300.
questions.explain: ₦600 is three ₦200s (greedy failed here), ₦900 is ₦500 + two ₦200s, and ₦300 cannot be made without ₦100s. Passing the count as a number (used) instead of an array of notes means there is nothing to undo.

questions.q: Ada and Bola must not sit next to each other. What does this print?
questions.explain: With three seats, Ada and Bola can only avoid each other if Chidi sits in the middle. Every order that puts Chidi at an end makes Ada and Bola neighbours, and the check prunes it as soon as the pair is formed.
options: ACB BCA
ABC ACB BAC BCA CAB CBA
ACB BCA CAB CBA
CAB CBA

questions.q: This counts the calls made while choosing 2 of 5 items, with and without the loop-bound prune. What does it print?
questions.explain: Without the bound, the first level also tries the last item (index 4) as the first pick, a call that can never be completed because no item is left after it. With i <= n - left, the loop stops when too few items remain. Here it saves one call; for "choose 10 of 30" it saves far more.
